column2: Act Fifteen
The Man Behind the Scenes
The Inside Man

“He's actually very lucky. Plenty of people help him. But there's something strange about it... It isn't happiness. None of that help ever makes him happy. It only keeps him precariously balanced on the edge of loneliness, as if he were the world's own child and no one dared let him truly despair. Whenever he's about to fall into the abyss of sorrow, someone always gives him a little comfort, like a handout, just enough to keep him going. I have a strange feeling... that on the day he truly despairs, he'll become...” Mai Sakatoku said softly, “something like a devil!”

Early morning, Beijing International Airport. The first flight of the day from North America to China had arrived, carrying an entire tour group. Customs hurriedly opened another entry lane, but a long line formed anyway. There was nothing these smartly dressed Americans could do but wait their turn. They all seemed well bred, except for a few noisy characters among them.
“Hey, Mingfei! Great to see you!” Someone from the tour group enthusiastically came forward to shake hands with Lu Mingfei, who had dark circles under both eyes.
“Townsend?” Lu Mingfei's eyes widened. The fellow had slept all night, completely unaware of what sort of company he was keeping.
“Wow, junior! You really do know everyone!” Fingel said.
“Are you here to slay a dragon too?” Townsend shook Fingel's hand as well.
“What do you mean... ‘too’?” Fingel suddenly realized that this was far more than a matter of a few hundred hybrids taking a group flight to China.

“That's right.” Townsend smiled and lowered his voice. “This is a special charter flight. We checked every passenger's identity in advance. They're all hybrids, without exception. We're all going to China to slay a dragon.”
“Isn't that a bit of an army?” Lu Mingfei and Fingel exclaimed together.

“We're all friends here. No need to hide it. Isn't that why you're here too? The news has spread like wildfire lately. I imagine every hybrid in the world knows a Dragon King may be waking in Beijing, unless they happen to be somewhere cut off from the news, like central Africa or the South American rain forest.”

“Come on, man! Who do you think you are? What qualifies you to go dragon-slaying in China? Do you think it's like visiting the World Expo? Buy a ticket, stand in line, and you're in?” Fingel gaped at him. “In that adorable little outfit?”

Instead of the formal suit he had worn at the auction, Townsend was dressed in a long-sleeved shirt under an army-green vest bristling with pockets, loose jeans, sneakers, and a New York Yankees baseball cap. Best of all, the shirt had bold Chinese calligraphy splashed across its chest: NO TRUE HERO UNTIL YOU REACH THE GREAT WALL.

“Oh.” Townsend gave a tolerant smile. “I'm not quite that unaware of my limitations. With my Yanling, never mind a Dragon King—even a second- or third-generation dragon would completely outclass me. I just thought it would be a shame not to witness such a momentous event... And you do have a point about the World Expo. It isn't over yet. My friends and I thought we could take a vacation in China and visit the Expo while we were here. Two birds with one stone, right? Look, some people have brought their whole families.”
“Hey, hey... What kind of fantastically laid-back middle-aged mindset lets you treat this as ‘I'll try my luck, and if it doesn't work out, it's a vacation’?”
“A hybrid born in 1977 is thirty-three this year. What's so strange about having a middle-aged mindset?”

At the same time, a Bombardier Global Express XRS touched down lightly at Capital Airport. It was a private aircraft arriving from Hong Kong, and unlike most private planes, it was painted solid black. Its door opened as soon as it stopped. Facing the wind and the rising sun, its distinguished passenger jumped straight out without waiting for the mobile stairs approaching the plane. Even on a midsize business jet, the door was more than two meters above the ground. What shocked the ground crew even more was that the passenger was wearing three-inch heels and carrying a large LV travel bag...

Mai Sakatoku lifted her face in the dawn light and pulled out her hair clip. Black hair spilled down like a waterfall. She stretched luxuriously, shaking off the fatigue of the journey. Every man watching instinctively touched his nose to see whether it was bleeding. Even seen only in silhouette against the dawn, every stretching curve of her body called to mind a flower opening into full bloom.

Chu Zihang was bent over his laptop. Lu Mingfei and Fingel were nodding off, their heads drooping. Only Townsend saw that unforgettable figure from behind. The girl in black leather ran past them and flashed through the deserted diplomatic lane like a streak of black light. He could not help whistling. Lu Mingfei raised his head in a daze. For an instant, he had caught a familiar scent: a delicate fragrance edged with the murderous chill of weapons.

A stretch Hummer waited outside the VIP exit. The driver, who doubled as a bodyguard and was dressed entirely in black, respectfully opened the door. Mai Sakatoku leaped into the cabin like a black swift taking flight. The door shut at once, and the Hummer sped away.

The rear cabin was a private space, completely partitioned off from the driver's seat, furnished in cherrywood and burgundy lambskin. Crystal glasses in the climate-controlled bar clinked as the vehicle swayed. A broad kangaroo-leather sofa faced a forty-two-inch LCD screen showing movements on the New York stock market. A girl curled on the enormous sofa wore black plastic-framed glasses; her long, chestnut-dyed hair hung over half her face. With one hand she rapidly scribbled on a sheet of paper, while the other held the car phone. Her voice was stern. “Raise the bid by 1.5 percent and buy all you can of the wind-energy companies we've selected! Your authorized limit is five hundred million dollars.” She grabbed a potato chip and stuffed it into her mouth. “Don't question my decision! Five minutes ago a two-hundred-thousand-ton tanker struck a reef and sank in the Gulf of Mexico. The spill will bring fierce environmentalist criticism of the oil economy. Alternative-energy companies will have enormous upside over the next three months!”
“Hey, Chips Girl! Looks like Beijing's treating you pretty well!” Mai Sakatoku dropped her travel bag and reached out to pinch the other girl's cheek.
“Hey! Hands to yourself!” Chips Girl hurriedly covered her face.

Too late. As a ninja, when Mai Sakatoku reached for someone's cheek, it was like drawing a blade to slit an enemy's throat: her hands always moved faster than words. Before Chips Girl could raise her hands, Mai had finished her pinch to her satisfaction and settled comfortably back on the sofa, taking off her sunglasses and crossing her legs.

“Letting a girl touch you won't kill you. You really have been looking after yourself. Your cheeks are so soft and smooth.” Mai looked her up and down. “Your clothes are still as frumpy as ever, though.”

“I put on a face mask while I was waiting for you...” Chips Girl looked down at her loose white shirt, faded blue jeans, and flat thong sandals. “I may not be in your league when it comes to fashion, but this isn't frumpy, okay? It's just a little casual.”

“Fuck! I've been hauling two swords all over the place in three-inch heels until my legs are ready to snap off, and you and the three-nothings girl have the nerve to live it up? Face masks? Casual? What kind of sweet little homebody buys five hundred million dollars' worth of wind-energy companies over the phone?” Mai rolled her eyes. “When you called, I didn't even put on makeup. I jumped into the car and raced to Kai Tak Airport. God knows how many red lights I ran or tickets I picked up. Meanwhile you're taking it easy.”
“Okay, okay, I know ‘babysitting’ is hard work. Once this job's over, you can take a long vacation.” Chips Girl hurried to soothe her. “Have you read the material I sent?”
“The bounty page on the Hunter Market? Yes. Whoever posted it knows how to play the game. They've played every hybrid in the world.”
“This plane arrived almost at the same time as yours. Three charter flights like it are flying from America to China within a week.” Chips Girl handed her a charter contract.

“Three Boeing 747-400s? North American hybrids certainly know how to spend.” Mai tossed the document back. “So more than a thousand hybrids have already entered China. Do they think dragon-slaying is some high-difficulty raid you can beat by throwing enough people at it? With some of their bloodlines, the instant they enter the domain of a dragon's majesty, they'll die of heart failure!”
“No, not a thousand. More than three thousand. Even more are coming to Beijing from Europe.”

Mai remembered something. “There were a few hundred people lined up inside when I left the airport. That must have been the group? If customs knew what kind of tour group they'd let into China, they'd probably be too horrified even to cry.”
“Three of them are named Fingel von Frings, Chu Zihang, and Lu Mingfei,” Chips Girl said.
Mai's expression grew grave. “Lu Mingfei's here? Then the boss has given us new orders?”

“I got an email from the boss three hours ago and called you right away,” Chips Girl said quietly. “The order is that, out of those three thousand people, Lu Mingfei must be the one to kill the Dragon King with his own hands!”

Mai put a hand to her forehead. “Here we go again! Is the boss a flake or a genius? Sometimes I really can't tell! Is that loser worth spending so much time on? What kind of ridiculous luck does he have? All these people playing nanny to him—it's like getting a wild card straight into the World Cup final! Characters this broken make you want to go over and kick them a couple of times!”

“We can't do anything about the boss's logic. Those are the orders.” Chips Girl's voice was utterly firm. “The Dragon King must die at Lu Mingfei's hands! Everyone else who sees the Dragon King will go to its grave with it!”

“Those really are charter flights to death.” Mai shrugged. “Fine. Let them be buried with it. Poor bastards. They can blame their luck for running into a freak like the boss. The problem is that Lu Mingfei really is useless. Otherwise, at the Three Gorges, he could have drawn Wrath and killed Norton instead of needing me to finish the job with that shot. How do we make sure he kills the Dragon King ‘with his own hands’?”

“We can still manage that. The six people from Cassell College have split into two teams, and Lu Mingfei's team has that set of alchemical blades. They're paradoxical weapons capable of slaughtering any Dragon King. All he needs is the will to draw them. There's another part of the order that's even harder.” Chips Girl sighed. “The fact that Lu Mingfei killed the Dragon King has to be made public.”
“Made public?” Mai froze. “What do you mean, made public? How can you make dragon-slaying public? Has the boss's brain short-circuited again?”
“‘I want the whole world... to watch his grand performance as a hero!’” Chips Girl enunciated each word. “That's the last sentence in the boss's letter.”

“Holy shit... Are we supposed to arrange a live broadcast on China Central Television?” Mai abruptly sat up straight, put both hands on her knees, and assumed a solemn, dignified expression. “Good evening, viewers. This is the Central People's Television evening news. Tonight's special report: ‘Requiem for a Dragon King in New China.’ We will now bring you live footage of Cassell College's S-rank loser, Lu Mingfei, battling the Dragon King. Over to our correspondent at the scene...”
“You really can turn it on at the drop of a hat. Could you stop clowning around, O People's Artist?” Chips Girl said helplessly.
“The whole world would go insane!” Mai was losing her mind.

“Anyway, you know the boss's style. His orders can't be disobeyed. However illogical they are, we have to let the whole world know that Lu Mingfei killed the Dragon King. The story has to appear in all the major media, even the national evening news.” Chips Girl patted Mai's shoulder comfortingly. “Now you see why I summoned you to Beijing in such a hurry. If we had time, I'd gladly sit here and cry with you. First we have to think of a way to handle this. You have the best media connections of any of us. What could I expect the three-nothings girl to come up with? She'd just faithfully carry out the boss's orders, shoot Lu Mingfei killing the dragon with a handheld camcorder, and upload it to YouTube or Tudou...”
“I can believe she'd do that...” Mai covered her face.
“Basically, we need to get a headline like ‘Lu Mingfei Successfully Kills Dragon King’ into the public media, without causing chaos...”
“Successfully kills... successfully kills... kills...” Mai's eyes lit up. She repeated the words several times, tasting the feel of the headline, then clapped her hands. “I've got it!”

“Let me guess. Not some lousy trick like buying the entire New York Times, printing a few million copies without putting them on sale, then destroying them?” Chips Girl stressed the point. “That won't fool the boss. It has to be released to the public.”

“Buying the entire New York Times would be a little expensive, wouldn't it? But I'll still need a budget of twelve million dollars... Actually, get me twenty million, just in case!” Mai bent down to fish her phone from her travel bag. “Two cashier's checks for ten million each.”

“Hey! Could you be a little less carefree and generous with the money? Every cent you people spend is something this poor bookkeeper worked her fingers to the bone to earn!” Chips Girl wailed as she took out the checks and began writing zeros. At the same time, her face broke into a delighted smile. “Still, that's a lot cheaper than I expected!”
Fourteen hours later. Blizzard headquarters, Irvine, California, USA.

Heber Hegarty, the head of marketing, pushed open the conference-room door. His unannounced visitor was already seated across the table, with the sunlight at his back. He was a young, handsome Chinese man who looked no older than thirty-five, impeccably dressed in a gray suit and matching tie, thoroughly proper and polite. Beside him sat a female secretary in a black skirt suit. He looked like a lawyer.

“Allow me to introduce myself. I'm an attorney practicing in Los Angeles. Our firm handles legal work relating to corporate mergers, breakups, refinancing, and public listings.” The Chinese man stood and offered a business card with a smile.

It was a celebrated law firm—or a notorious one. These wolfish attorneys pursued cash-strapped companies around the Bay Area, sinking their teeth into them and profiting by tearing them apart and selling the pieces on the market. Behind them stood massive institutions with enormous sums at their disposal.
“How do you do? May I ask the purpose of your visit...?” Heber smiled cautiously. Representatives of financial institutions like these were not people to offend lightly.

The lawyer took an envelope from his assistant, laid it on the table, and pushed it toward Heber. “This is a cashier's check for ten million dollars. One of our clients is very interested in your online game World of Warcraft...”

Heber stared. “I'm sorry, but World of Warcraft is our core source of profits. Ten million dollars would be nowhere near enough either to buy the game or to acquire a stake in Blizzard.” Inwardly, he scoffed at the lawyer's ignorance. Did he think he could mount an attack on Blizzard armed with a ten-million-dollar check?

The lawyer smiled. “You may have misunderstood. We're not here about a merger or a breakup this time. We're representing a client who wishes to commission a new ‘dungeon’ for World of Warcraft, to be developed within seven days. Its story must follow a script supplied by our client. Development must be completed and the update installed on servers worldwide within seven days. Beyond that, we seek no rights to the dungeon.”

Heber was stunned. The piece of paper worth ten million dollars seemed to burn his hands through the envelope. The offer was far too generous. Ten million was enough to develop a major online game, and all they wanted was a single dungeon. He could not tell whether this was a trap.

Seeing his hesitation, the lawyer smiled with a sigh. “Yes, it sounds absurd. But as a law firm, we can hardly refuse a major client's requests. I received a late-night call from a client in Asia. She said she was a devoted World of Warcraft player and very much wanted a custom-designed, high-difficulty dungeon, along with the honor of the ‘first kill.’” He shrugged. “I don't play games. I only learned on the drive over, after searching online, that a ‘first kill’ counts as an honor.”

“Yes. When certain difficult dungeons are released, guilds on the server compete to see who can kill the boss first. Once they've achieved the first kill, they usually post a screenshot of the victory online to announce their accomplishment. The server also immediately sends the news to every player. Players all over the world pay attention.”

“Sounds like the honor the guys competed for when I was at Yale... being the first to date the prettiest girl in the law school,” the lawyer said. “Ten million dollars for an honor. I'd say that's quite a good deal for you.”
Heber hesitated. “But sir, developing a new dungeon is simply not something that can be done in seven days...”

“Then I'll add another check for ten million.” Plainly unwilling to waste words, the lawyer cut him off and held out his right hand. His assistant handed him another envelope without a change of expression.
“Twenty million dollars for an honor.” The lawyer was as cold as a tyrant.
The silence lasted half a minute.

“All right. You win. But before we sign, I'd like to know what your script is.” Heber nodded. Twenty million dollars could buy a luxury yacht to cross the Atlantic. Naturally, it could also buy seven days of overtime from Blizzard's entire staff.

“I've brought the fax. The client wrote the script personally.” The lawyer cleared his throat. “Fenrisulfr is a giant dragon inhabiting the wilds of the East. Usually it does nothing but sleep. When it wakes, it flies to a castle and carries off the princess... There's a note here: ‘Any castle will do, but please don't have it carry off a troll princess or anything. That would look too ridiculous.’”
“Is your client really a devoted World of Warcraft player?” Heber gaped. “That's completely incompatible with Warcraft lore! What alternate universe is this?”
“Please let me finish... After taking the princess, Fenrisulfr discovers that this beautiful girl belongs to a different species and cannot become its wife, so it eats her...”
Heber rubbed his face hard and took a deep breath, urging himself to keep listening for the sake of the twenty million dollars.

“The king is heartbroken and posts a proclamation seeking brave warriors to avenge his daughter. Many young men therefore set out on the quest... Here, Fenrisulfr has an extremely bad temper. Whenever anyone tries to disturb its sleep, it flies into a rage and destroys everything around it. That makes it very hard to kill. The heroes must obtain a sacred item called the Seven Deadly Sins. This is a weapon for punishing every form of evil, a set of seven pieces, each bearing a different inscription. Together they form an ancient incantation.” The lawyer took off his glasses and slowly recited, “‘All royal blood shall end by the sword!’”

Heber thought for a moment. “All right. The script is a little different in style, but it's doable. I must stress one thing, though. We can develop the dungeon for you, but we can't guarantee that your client will get the ‘first kill.’ Once the dungeon is released, the dragon's lair will be open to every player on the server.”
“You only need to develop it according to the contract. Slaying the dragon is our business,” the lawyer said mildly.
“All right. I'll have the contract prepared now.” Heber stood, hesitating slightly. “But I have to be honest. Your client may have a gaming addiction. It's an illness... it needs treatment.”

The lawyer sighed softly. “Actually, I don't know the client personally either. The person who contacted us is only a subordinate. I hear he's a shut-in gamer with a terrible temper. Once, because he was unhappy with the leveling system in Final Fantasy XIV, he dumped a huge quantity of Square stock... You have no idea how hard it is to cater to these rich people. Sometimes they're positively neurotic.”

Thirty minutes later, the lawyer drove off in his Porsche sports car with his pretty assistant, having gotten exactly what he wanted. Lying across the backseat was a friendly gift from Heber: a full-size replica of the greatsword Frostmourne.
Beijing, China.

Old Luo quietly wiped his sweaty hands on his pants and stared at the tabletop. The open case on it held neat stacks of cash with the bank bands still intact. Going out late at night with so much cash was astonishing enough. More astonishing was that they had arranged to meet in a Chengdu Snacks restaurant. Most astonishing of all, of course, was the girl sitting across the table. She simply did not belong in a cheap little eatery like this. Her fitted black leather clothes flaunted every curve. Through the open neckline, a tiny bandeau top and slim, straight collarbones were visible. Her jet-black hair shone like a mirror, tied with a red cord into the high coiffure of a lady from an ancient painting. An expensive fragrance enveloped her.

A touch of crimson shaded the corners of her eyes. Clear black pupils gazed deep into Old Luo's. Her rose-red lips parted and closed as though murmuring the most intimate secrets between lovers... In fact, she was gnawing on a skewer of grilled kidney.
Everyone in the little restaurant was watching the girl eat kidney. When she ordered, she had set a case full of cash on the table, pulled out a bill, and handed it to the waiter. “Double the chili.”

“I only have seven days. I need a max-level character with the best gear and skills, and the best team behind him. I mean he needs to be the leader of a major guild. Top-tier priests, warriors who can tank, druids who can double as healers—give him two sets of everything. His ID is ‘Lu Mingfei Ricardo.’” Mai set down her bamboo skewer and began leisurely filing her nails. “Can you do it? Everyone says you're the best in the business.” She mischievously narrowed one eye at Old Luo. “Hey, hero, stop staring at the money. It'll all be yours. Look up at me.”

Old Luo led one of the top guilds on World of Warcraft's Chinese servers. In the virtual world, he was a blood elf paladin with the ID “White North,” a conqueror who stormed cities and seized territory, a mighty lord who threw money around by the handful. Join his guild and he would buy you a horse and give you a dragon. Under his rule, the guild had become an empire. He was the kind of character who led a raid to slaughter the Lich King while posting long poems in guild chat. As the Lich King crashed to the ground, Old Luo would unhurriedly fill the channel with Rilke's “Orpheus. Eurydice. Hermes.”: “This was the mine of souls, obscure and remote. Silently they passed through the dark, like hidden veins of silver. Blood welled between the roots of stone and flowed toward the world of men; in the endless night, it lay heavy as rock. Beyond it, nothing red remained.” Girls worshipped his style. They imagined a cold young man driving an eight-horse chariot down a long street, cracking a whip that tore the clothes of girls who hid from him yet stole glances at him, leaving scarlet marks on their lovely skin as he threw back his head and laughed.

Everyone who knew Old Luo called him “boss,” though he looked more like the owner of an internet café. His supposedly devil-may-care jacket had gone unwashed for two weeks; his hair was full of dandruff and stuck straight up like a bird's nest. But he was the sort of man who became an emperor the moment he sat before a screen and touched a keyboard. Whenever he entered an internet café, dropped twenty yuan on the counter, and murmured, “All night. A Nutri-Express and a pack of Zhongnanhai,” the Warcraft players around him would raise their heads to look at this star-bright veteran. For the rest of the night they could admire his dashing form curled on a sofa with a strange little smile, his left hand playing the keyboard like Beethoven, his right hand holding a cigarette as he wielded the mouse like a master of wild cursive calligraphy.
“No problem! What race and class?” Old Luo's expression was resolute.

“Human. Male. Black hair. A sad little kid's face. Useless-looking. Definitely not too handsome.” Mai handed him a black-and-white photograph. “Make him look like this. As for class... a rogue, I guess. He's always been a petty thief.”
“Not much personality for a hero,” Old Luo tutted.

Mai clapped her hands. The black-clad driver came in carrying a paper guillotine. Before anyone could react, she stood up with a skewer of grilled tendon between her teeth, picked up a stack of cash, and chopped it in half.
After a moment's silence, a happily drunk fellow clapped. “Attagirl!”

Amid whistles and cheers, Mai's long hair swayed as she cut another stack in two, and another, and another. Each downward stroke of the blade had a graceful rhythm. Half banknotes fluttered into the travel bag the driver had set down.

“A five-hundred-thousand-yuan advance.” Mai zipped up the bag and pushed it toward Old Luo. “I'm giving you all the right halves. You won't be able to exchange them for whole bills at the bank. If you want the left halves, bring me the character. Work hard, sweetheart. You're adorable... But remember to wash your hair properly before you see me again! I can feel a fermented smell drifting over from your side!”

She blew a flirtatious glance at everyone present, took five thousand yuan from her wallet, and laid it on the table. “Tonight's drinks are on me. In seven days, go online and watch a man named Lu Mingfei kill a giant dragon.”

To cheers, she swayed gracefully toward the stretch Hummer outside. Before getting in and leaving, she turned and waved, exactly like a movie star bidding the press farewell after her own awards gala. Yet no one thought it odd that this was happening outside a Chengdu Snacks restaurant. Everyone sensed that something big was about to happen, something thrilling to look forward to. They raised their beer bottles to see off this thoroughly amazing girl.

“Over the next seven days,” Old Luo told his deputy guild leader on the phone, “we're going to build a gleaming, golden Lu Mingfei at number one on the rankings! Yes... he's going to kill that dragon!”
“Hey, Legs. Will this really work?” Chips Girl leaned against the window, looking out.

It was sunrise. Fiery clouds burned along the horizon, and the sun slowly floated up like a cooked egg yolk. Traffic was thickening on the ring road below. A new day had begun. In this top-floor conference room in the heart of the central business district, she and Mai had gone twenty-four hours without sleep. All other business had stopped. The New York stockbroker had not received a call from Chips Girl in a whole day. He was wondering whether his client had been kidnapped, and whether he ought to call the police.

“It should, provided every stage connects smoothly. Blizzard has canceled all employee vacations. For the next seven days, they'll work in two shifts, developing around the clock. The announcement of the new dungeon will go up on Blizzard's official website in a few hours. Launch is set for seven days from now.” Mai glanced at her watch. “No, six days and four hours. It'll be the first time in Blizzard's history that a release hasn't been delayed. That Old Luo fellow is doing well too. ‘Lu Mingfei Ricardo’ has already reached level fifty-seven. Two teams are taking turns leveling him, with two more providing support. By noon today he'll be at max level. Over the next few days, he'll cover the entire map collecting skill points, reputation, and top-tier items. When the dungeon goes live, one of the top-ranked heroes will be standing at its entrance.”

Three thirty-six-inch HD screens stood directly before Mai and to either side. Linked together, they provided a nearly 180-degree view. An endless swamp stretched across them, with crocodiles dimly visible here and there. A little rogue was riding through the mud on horseback, the words “Lu Mingfei Ricardo” floating over his head. In fact, he was far from alone. Zoom out a little and you would discover behind him... a surging cavalry corps. Max-level tanks and powerful healers thronged around him. Guild chat raced past: “Hurry, tell Old Bai to go farm that dagger for Brother Lu!” “Who's meeting Brother Lu in Stormwind? Fly over there. Our main force is almost there.” “We need a hundred and twenty wool cloth. Get it for Brother Lu!” “Hey, boss. They asked for a max-level character. Should we max out Brother Lu's cooking too?”
“This looks so lively I'm tempted to make an account myself.” Mai nudged the wireless mouse.
“What about the media?” Chips Girl asked.

“I held a press conference at the Kempinski last night and invited every media outlet in the industry. I handed out five hundred red envelopes with two hundred dollars in each. The instant we get the first kill, the reporters who took our envelopes will post the story on every major gaming website. The headline is settled: ‘Lu Mingfei's Team Scores First Kill of Dragon King.’ A few hours later, the city papers will race to reprint it. A few hours after that, it'll be on the television news. I even contacted a publisher who'll put out a nonfiction novel.”

“All that's missing is a movie with the same title...” Chips Girl raised her eyebrows. “Mobilizing all those resources just to make one big boy happy? Tell me, Mai, do you think the boss really cares how Lu Mingfei feels?”
Mai thought for a moment and shook her head. “I don't think he cares how anyone feels.”
“That's what I think too. You've spent time with Lu Mingfei. What kind of person is he, really?”

“It's hard to say. On the surface he seems like a coward. He has no confidence in himself and no expectations, so he doesn't try very hard at anything.” Mai put her feet on the conference table and held a mug of hot chocolate, gazing absently at the ceiling. “But sometimes he turns into someone else... lonely and vicious, with so much refusal to give in hidden in his eyes. It's like... he's caught fire.”
“Wildfires start burning deep in the heart, don't they?” Chips Girl said softly.

Mai took a sip of hot chocolate. “He's actually very lucky. Plenty of people help him. But there's something strange about it... It isn't happiness. None of that help ever makes him happy. It only keeps him precariously balanced on the edge of loneliness, as if he were the world's own child and no one dared let him truly despair. Whenever he's about to fall into the abyss of sorrow, someone always gives him a little comfort, like a handout, just enough to keep him going. I have a strange feeling... that on the day he truly despairs, he'll become...” Mai Sakatoku said softly, “something like a devil!”

The fluorescent tubes were shrouded in choking smoke. People cheered or cursed from time to time, while others, headsets on, poured out tender feelings to girls at the other end. A hundred-odd computers stood in rows. On every broken-down sofa sat a red-eyed fellow who had paid for the night, a cigarette in his left hand and a mouse in his right. Hard-driving rock leaked from cheap headphones. As usual, the girl at the cash register was fast asleep. All the noise and all the faces of joy and sorrow in the world seemed gathered here, in an underground internet café in Chaoyang District.

The man who was supposedly going to burn the world with the fire in his heart, Lu Mingfei, was directing his army of Dragoons onto the high ground. Zealots bearing psi blades formed ranks behind them. Golden Reavers crawled slowly forward, while High Templars cloaked in blue lightning hovered in the air.

The enemy's main base sat on the high ground: a typical Terran fortress. Its buildings were packed tightly into an orderly layout. Rows of Supply Depots stood at the front, followed by Bunkers full of Marines and, farther back, masses of tanks deployed in Siege Mode. Squadrons of Valkyries patrolled around the base. Missile Turret radar covered every area to keep Lu Mingfei's Dark Templars from slipping through in the confusion.
This was the final battle. The enemy had raised an iron wall before Lu Mingfei's army.

This was the fifteenth challenger to take him on tonight. The previous fourteen had all been beaten so badly they were crying for mercy. Some had hurled their keyboards down and cursed; others muttered to themselves as though they had attained enlightenment.

The StarCraft crowd in the café was stunned. Where had this brat come from, drinking Coke with his eyebrows drooping as he routed them all? Worst of all, sometimes he would switch the mouse to his left hand so he could scratch an itch. To the StarCraft experts, this was sheer humiliation. It was like Ximen Chuixue meeting Ye Gucheng to duel atop the Forbidden City, except Ximen Chuixue had brought a rake instead of a sword and still beaten Ye Gucheng to a pulp. There would be no way for Ye to save face short of cutting his own throat.

Was he here to challenge the whole establishment? They had no choice but to call Brother Dog. Brother Dog was the undisputed grandmaster here, so far above the rest of the world that he had no worthy opponent. In his own words, he was “so lonely at the top, all I can do is go home and put the kid to bed.”

Brother Dog was astonished. It was the happiness of Dugu Qiubai, the Seeker of Defeat, suddenly discovering that he lived in the same age as Dongfang Bubai, the Invincible East. He hurriedly knelt on a washboard for a while to persuade his wife to watch their child that night, then rushed over in his slippers.
The moment he entered, he was knocked senseless by a club. Then came six more blows in rapid succession. Brother Dog lost seven straight games without the slightest ability to fight back.

Only then did he understand that he was not living in the same age as Dongfang Bubai at all... He was living in the age of the Transformers. Your black-iron greatsword might embody the supreme elegance of simplicity, but when it hit the enemy, all it produced was a few clangs before the other fellow flattened you with one foot.

For this game, Brother Dog had thrown everything into mounting an unprecedented defensive stand at his own base. Whatever trickery Lu Mingfei tried, he was confident he had two answers ready. A brute-force Carrier assault, an airborne drop in the confusion, a flood of Zealots—Brother Dog was prepared to make any of them bleed rivers! He felt his adrenaline surge to the limit. The hand gripping his mouse trembled slightly. He was a general on horseback with his blade held crosswise, aching to roar at the formidable enemy across from him: “Come on!”
But across from him was only a brat with drooping eyebrows and a listless expression. Lu Mingfei drank the last of his Coke, made a few casual inputs, and got up to go to the restroom.
Brother Dog was dumbfounded. What was this? Surrender? If he was surrendering, he could at least type “GG”!
“Nuclear launch detected.” The cold warning sounded in his headphones.

Brother Dog froze. What was going on? Nuclear missiles were Terran weapons, but Lu Mingfei was playing Protoss! Of course, Protoss could use a Dark Archon to capture a Protoss worker and thereby reproduce a Terran army, but did anyone actually play that way? Hardly anyone even built top-tier units like Dark Archons, did they? And even after capturing a worker, wouldn't it take ages to reproduce the entire Terran building tree? What kind of lunatic played like this? Wasn't this a strategy that existed only in theory?
“Nuclear launch detected.” Another warning. It was not a repeat. Another nuclear missile had been launched.
“Nuclear launch detected.”
“Nuclear launch detected.”
“Nuclear launch detected.”
“Nuclear launch detected.”

Six warnings in succession. Almost simultaneously, Lu Mingfei had launched six nuclear missiles! Brother Dog dragged his mouse around, frantically searching the screen for the red targeting dots. Too late. The six nukes slammed down one after another. His disciplined formations and ironclad defenses vanished. The base he had so painstakingly built was reduced to ruins. The few remaining buildings had red health bars and blazed with fire. Meanwhile, Lu Mingfei's great army... was simply drawn up outside, doing nothing, in the shape of an enormous V.
So Lu Mingfei had built an entire screenful of troops just to make a V!
When Lu Mingfei came back from the restroom, he saw “GG” on the screen. A few seconds later, Brother Dog quit.
“Master... how about one more? I'd like to learn.” Brother Dog walked over and spoke sincerely. “Boss, two Nutri-Expresses.”
The owner set the drinks in front of him. Brother Dog glared. “Just one for me. The other's for the master over there. Beating us up is thirsty work.”
“Thanks, thanks. Sure, sure,” Lu Mingfei said.
“Mind if we watch from behind you, man?” Someone edged over.
“Sure, sure,” Lu Mingfei said.

And so another game began, this time as a lesson. A crowd gathered behind Lu Mingfei. A rather pretty girl in a little black dress sat beside him, her eyes wide with curiosity. At this moment, Lu Mingfei was the star of the place. Embarrassed, he shifted his butt to avoid brushing against her thigh. But inwardly, he was a little thrilled...
Was this what people called feeling that you mattered?

Some people felt they mattered beside champagne-soaked swimming pools, amid streams of luxury cars and clouds of beautiful women. That was Caesar. Some felt it on dragon-slaying battlefields where blood ran in rivers. That was Chu Zihang. Some felt it ringing a bell and showing off to the Board of Trustees. That was Anjou. Some found it in erguotou liquor and lingerie magazines. That was the vice principal... And he found it in internet cafés like this one, filthy and shabby, thick with smoke and dimly lit, with the occasional girl showing her legs. Everyone would glance back as if by accident... Yet only here did he feel that someone might care what he was.

“This is the story of a man who has yet to realize his destiny—” Sound leaked from the headphones of the guy beside him, who was watching anime. The hot-blooded hero on screen—it was the Taiwanese dub, with something of the grandiose delivery of Pili puppet theater—pointed at the sky and shouted.
“Let's head for the surface, Simon!”
“Kamina...”
“What do you mean, Kamina? Call me big bro!”
“But I... don't have any brothers...”
“That's not what I mean! I mean a brother of the soul, a soul brother! Don't mind what those ugly girls say. This thing suits you. Your drill is your soul!”

That was Gurren Lagann, wasn't it? The idiot big brother, bursting with fighting spirit, who would take on giant robots with a Japanese sword, was lecturing his useless little brother. Watching it before had made his blood boil with excitement. Hearing it now... what kind of lines were those? Your drill is your soul? So the mouse was Lu Mingfei's soul, and a red-wine bottle was Fingel's? Souls sure differed from person to person... It must be late outside now. Nono and Caesar... what were they doing?

His fingers danced over the keyboard. His army took shape once more. Zealots gathered into a torrent of steel, psi blades flickering. Dragoons danced. Carriers massed together. The screen's glow lit his blank face.

The executive suite was a wreck. Papers littered the floor, several laptops were running, and a map of Beijing was projected on the wall. Brightly colored fast-food wrappers lay everywhere too, with two half-eaten family buckets on the table.
Chu Zihang sat upright at the table, typing with a chocolate bar between his teeth. He had worked without stopping since checking into the hotel, subsisting on chocolate bars, cookies, and soda.
Fingel sprawled amid the papers covering the bed, a bottle of red wine in one hand and a fried chicken drumstick in the other, as contented as a toad lying belly-up in the sun.
“Lu Mingfei's been out all day. Do you know where he went?” Chu Zihang asked suddenly.
“Said he was going to an internet café. Gaming here would disturb your work. Junior, we're counting on you. The other team is all elite, and you're stuck dragging us two stepchildren around.”
“I think you've misunderstood that expression. In Chinese, it means the child a divorced woman had with her former husband,” Chu Zihang corrected him. “For example, I'm one.”

Chu Zihang pressed Enter, loading the data into the mathematical model he had just finished. Countless ripples spread across the projected map on the wall in an instant, as though it were a still lake and he had just scattered a handful of fine sand onto it.

“What are you tinkering with?” Fingel could not make sense of it. “Didn't we come here to slay a dragon? Yet all three of us are shut-ins in our own way. Our useless junior's a gaming nerd, you're a science nerd, and I'm a... I'm a glutton. Shouldn't we be hauling equipment all over Beijing looking for a dragon?”

“If by equipment you mean DSLR cameras, Townsend and his friends are doing exactly that. They visited the Forbidden City yesterday. Today's destination is the Summer Palace,” Chu Zihang said evenly. “The reason they've turned into a tour group through and through is that they've discovered dragon traces everywhere in this city. There are dragon veins in the landscape, auspicious dragons and phoenixes on imperial stone carvings, dragons' descendants crouched on every corner of the halls. Even the tortoises carrying stone steles are dragon offspring. There's nowhere to begin. China uses the dragon as its totem, so it ought to preserve the most information about dragons. But all that jumbled information hides the essential information we're looking for.” He pointed his pencil at the patches of ripples on the map. “The jumbled information I have now is this year's ground-motion data for Beijing and the surrounding area.”
“Ground-motion data?”

“The seismological bureau has installed a lot of small monitoring devices throughout the city. Beijing lies on the Yanshan seismic belt in North China. There are hundreds of small earthquakes every year, but their magnitude and intensity are so low that we can't even feel them. The instruments faithfully record every movement, though. It might be a shift in the earth's crust, or it might be something hiding inside it. This year, the frequency of ground movements in Beijing suddenly increased tenfold. I've built a simple mathematical model and fed the data into it. Using various calculations and filters, we may be able to locate the source: the King of Earth and Mountain.”
Fingel listened blankly for a long while, then nodded. “That's amazing!”
“It's natural that you don't understand. My courses lean toward science, yours toward dragon genealogy,” Chu Zihang said mildly. “In other words, I'm a science major and you're a humanities major.”

“Fuck, nine years in college before I find out I'm a humanities major!” Fingel took a swig of wine. “So this bad-tempered Dragon King keeps firing off his powers from one spot? What if he's moving while he does it?”
“Why would a Dragon King move? Does he have a job to go to?”
“True. He should be hiding somewhere building up his strength, so he can knock us all flat once he's fully recovered.” Fingel nodded. “So this data will put us ahead of Caesar's team?”

“Hard to say. Too many things cause ground vibrations in a city: heavy trucks, subway trains, construction machinery, even fireworks during festivals. Those all get recorded too. In other words, the ground-motion data is mixed with hundreds of times as much irrelevant data. There's no telling how long it will take to filter it out, and our time is limited.” Chu Zihang stared at the projection. “Senior, have you ever had a girlfriend?”
“Hey... what kind of conversational hairpin turn is that? Don't you need some connection between one thing and the next? You science guys really are a bunch of blockheads!” Fingel jumped.
“Sorry. It just occurred to me. If you'd rather not answer, that's fine.”

“Why wouldn't I answer? It's my glorious military history! An immortal monument on the battlefield of love!” Fingel sat bolt upright. “I used to be an A-rank everyone adored! In my first few years at college, I was a hero like you, wandering among the flowers and conquering wherever I went! Girls who admired me lined up to give me chocolates on Valentine's Day. There were so many I had to melt them down into chocolate spread. Enough for a whole year's breakfast toast!”
“So you did have a girlfriend? And then you broke up?” Chu Zihang looked at him seriously.
“You've hit a sore spot!” Fingel clutched his chest.
“Sorry. I just wanted some advice... If you liked a girl and had never told her, and now she was about to marry someone, would you tell her?”
“You're worried about that loser's mental health?” Fingel understood. “I suppose I wouldn't tell her...”
“Then you'd make the same choice as Lu Mingfei.” Thoughtfully, Chu Zihang opened a can of Coke.
“Why would I tell her?” Fingel glared. “I'd choose to take out the groom first!”
Chu Zihang considered this for a few seconds. “If he doesn't say anything, those hidden feelings are worth nothing. One day he'll die with them, and no one will even know. So why not tell her?”

Fingel flopped backward onto the bed again. “Feelings are funny things. Some people's are worth a fortune, and some people's are garbage. Our useless junior's, for instance, aren't worth a cent. He can't give Nono anything Caesar can. Love is a sacred word, but it isn't hard currency. You can't exchange it for food. Don't think your feelings are precious just because you like someone, my friend. The sooner he forgets that useless love of his, the better.”
“But you just said you'd take out the groom.”

“Everyone's different. Take a lunatic like you. If you fell for a girl, it would shake heaven and earth. If she was marrying someone else, even if the wedding car had already left, you'd blast the axle apart and steal her away,” Fingel said. “But our useless junior's a wimp. Even if Caesar invited him to be best man, he wouldn't know how to refuse. He'd stand behind Nono in a crisp suit and watch her marry into the Gattuso family, then come back, down two bottles of red wine, and sleep like a dead pig. The fiercest he gets is charging into hordes of zombies with a shotgun in Resident Evil, drooling as he blasts them.”
“Love has no value unless it drives you mad?”
“You could put it that way.” Fingel shook his head and sighed. “A coward who can only burn in secret and never dares do anything—his love is cheap! No, not cheap. He's a complete fucking idiot!”

“A complete fucking idiot?” Chu Zihang weighed the phrase. “What sort of person qualifies as a complete fucking idiot? I know it's an insult, but it seems you can call anyone that. Does it have a specific meaning?” He was fastidious about language. Almost anything he said could be printed unabridged in a middle-school textbook—a science textbook, at that. He stated facts in a wholly level tone, without the slightest inflection.

“Well...” Fingel scratched his tangled hair. “A Chinese guy asking a German to explain ‘a complete fucking idiot’ is already pretty fucking... Anyway, the phrase basically covers any irritating loser you look down on. In our junior's case, I guess it means... someone who knows something's impossible but insists on hanging on to hope. He's a coward all the time, then sometimes this thing gets his blood up and he acts like a lunatic, but when the moment comes for him to be brave, he chickens out again... Just a clueless little brat, stubborn as fuck and spineless too. Jesus! He's got every flaw in the book. Doesn't that make him a complete fucking idiot?”
Chu Zihang was silent for a long time, then nodded slightly. “I understand. He is a complete fucking idiot. So, senior, how did you break up with your girlfriend?”

“Fuck! Another hairpin turn! It's like asking a specialist about cosmetic surgery and having him suddenly ask whether you still have your appendix!” Fingel grumbled. “All right. It was because I was a complete fucking idiot back then too...”
“Everyone's a complete fucking idiot sometimes, aren't they?” Chu Zihang said quietly.
A knock sounded at the door, followed by a pinched voice. “Mole, Mole, this is Sweet Potato!”

Chu Zihang got up to open the door. Xia Mi poked her head inside, laden with bags, and gestured to Fingel. “Wow, what a mess! Is this the legendary boys' dorm room? The kind where you keep cockroaches as pets? May I come in? Could you ask your pets to move aside first? I'm afraid I'll step on the cute little creatures...”

She wore a long, Bohemian-style plaid skirt, straight-shaft deerskin boots, and a cropped burgundy sheepskin jacket, with a long purple scarf wound around her neck. No one could pin down her style. Every time they saw her, she looked striking in a different way. Presumably she had a whole walk-in closet full of clothes to compare and mix and match.
“Our junior's so pretty! Come let your senior see whether your waist has grown...” Fingel spread his arms wide.
Xia Mi smashed a piece of cheesecake into his face. “I brought you food so you wouldn't starve to death! Huh? Where's Lu Mingfei?”

“Your senior Lu has gone off to train in the outside world. He won't be back for a while. We'll meet again in the Sabaody Archipelago in two years. Just split his food between us. Is it Beijing street food?” Fingel's eyes shone.

“Yep, yep.” Xia Mi sat down and rummaged through the bags. “I'm from Beijing, you know. I'm going home to see Mom and Dad today, so I went shopping and picked up some food for you while I was at it. There are two Chinese guys on your team, but somehow you look like the one who's best at taking care of himself, Fingel.”
“You flatter me. Just the survival instinct to find food wherever I go. Born with it.” Fingel looked pleased with himself.

“Daoxiangcun pastries, candied fruit, Eighteenth Street fried dough twists... those are from Tianjin... and Tianfuhao pork knuckle.” Xia Mi took them out one by one. “Enough to feed you for a few days.”
Fingel pressed a hand to his chest. “Ah! This overwhelming happiness! You really are our team's undercover agent, aren't you? I knew your heart was still on our side.”
“Because you're the handsomest senior, Fingel.” Xia Mi grinned, baring her teeth.
Fingel turned to Chu Zihang and thumped his chest. “See, junior? You still need your senior's looks to rescue you from the misery of eating junk food all day!”
Chu Zihang could not be bothered with these two clowns. After nodding a greeting to Xia Mi, he had kept his eyes on the map of Beijing, lost in thought.
“Beijing's ground-motion data?” Xia Mi came to stand beside him. Her major leaned toward science, and she understood at a glance.

Chu Zihang nodded. “But there's too much junk data. Too much interference. It's like wind rippling a lake: with waves everywhere, we can't find the bubbles from that one fish.” He tapped the map. “That fish is hiding under the surface. On the day it fully wakes, it'll suddenly burst out of the water in dragon form. By then it'll be too late.”
“He's still in human form at present. To wake completely, he should be in the process of transforming into a dragon's body,” Xia Mi said.

“Yes. Otherwise he couldn't have caused the incidents at South Railway Station and Six Flags. He could hardly have flown to America in dragon form,” Chu Zihang said. “But a dragon in human form has limited power. The Dragon King Norton already proved that.”

Xia Mi studied the map. “Transforming completely into a dragon takes time. It's like going through incubation again. I told Mom and Dad how well you've looked after me, and they said they'd like to invite you home for a meal.”

Chu Zihang froze. Before he could answer, Fingel's booming voice broke in. “Another science-major conversational hairpin turn? Hey, hey, is this the legendary ‘meeting the parents’?” He covered his face. “This is shamefully adorable!”
“Adorable, my ass!” Xia Mi whipped around and snarled. “It's just an invitation to dinner!”
“Then why aren't I invited?” Fingel jumped up to demand.
Xia Mi froze.

“Obviously I'm not! You clearly never meant to invite me! Guilty conscience! You're blushing! Damn it! I knew you little girls thought of your senior as a middle-aged man! All that ‘you're the handsomest’ stuff was a lie!” Fingel was furious.
“I don't know you...” Xia Mi covered her face and turned away.
Chu Zihang coughed and hesitated for a few seconds. “As you can see, we're swamped here. I probably won't have time to visit. Please thank your parents for their kindness.”

“It's only a meal. Surely you can spare a few hours. My brother really wanted to meet you when he heard about you.” Xia Mi covered her ears. “On the phone he kept yelling, ‘Sis, Sis, I want big brother to come play with me!’ So noisy, so noisy, so noisy! I had no choice but to come invite you!” She leaned her face close to Chu Zihang's. “Do me the honor? Please? Please?” Her head bobbed and her eyes rolled about.
“I...” Chu Zihang was at a loss. “I'm not very good at playing with people...”
“Isn't he your older brother? Why does he call you big sister? And didn't you say before that he was your little brother?” Fingel was curious.

“It's ‘big sister’ as in the mature-woman type!” Xia Mi stuck out her tongue. “He's been a little slow to develop since birth, so mentally he's like a child. That's why he always thinks I'm his big sister.”
“Come to think of it, helping minors is a time-honored virtue at Cassell College!” Fingel puffed out his chest. “It's my bounden duty! And yours too, Chu Zihang!”
Chu Zihang had no choice. “When?”
“Lunch, three days from now? How about we make dumplings?”
“All right.” Chu Zihang nodded.

“Oh dear! But I already have plans for lunch that day,” Fingel suddenly said. “Much as I'd love to go with you, the timing's unfortunate. You'll have to go to our junior's house for the meal yourself.”
Chu Zihang stared. “What... plans?”
Fingel shook out his fluffy long hair to give it a touch of artistic individuality, straightened his clothes, and raised his chin. “A visit to Beijing's 798 Art District.”
“You're screwing with me, aren't you?” Chu Zihang thought.

“Oh, you're going to 798? There are a few good galleries there. I'll draw you a map...” Xia Mi was already sitting on the bed, sketching a map for Fingel on a sheet of white paper. No one paid Chu Zihang any further attention, as though everything were settled, perfectly natural and reasonable. At noon three days from now, duty-bound Chu Zihang would represent Cassell College, that aristocratic institution with its fine tradition of moral virtues, at lunch in Xia Mi's home, and play with her older brother.

Chu Zihang suddenly understood why people kept typing “table flip” online. It was that feeling of wanting to smash a keyboard into these two people's faces! It had been a con from the beginning! Since when did Cassell College have a tradition of helping minors? When had that bunch of killing machines ever given a damn about minors?
“Hey, undercover junior, what's Caesar up to?” Fingel suddenly asked.
“Since yesterday, I think he's mostly been drinking tea, taking Finnish saunas, getting spa treatments, that sort of thing. Today I think he went browsing in Liulichang.”
